The specimens were rinsed thoroughly in alcohol and acetone and dried before weighing to determine the pre-exposed weight measurement of the samples. To conduct the tests, Element 16 team built an experimental facility to fill sulfur inside mini pressure vessel envelopes loaded with corrosion coupons in an inert gas purged environment. The test envelope design involved 2” pipe with welded pipe cap on one end and a 2” class 150 socket connect union with welded plate on the other end for sealing as shown in Figure 5. A custom coupon holder that can hold multiple replicates of each material was fabricated (Figure 6). Figure 7 shows photographs of the oven, test envelopes and corrosion coupons. The sealed sulfur envelopes were then subjected to isothermal testing, based on expert feedback, in molten sulfur at 300 oC for a maximum duration of 2000 hours at Element 16 facility. The corrosion coupons were removed at different time intervals and sent to Intertek for measurement and analysis of corrosion depth, metal loss rates and tensile strength. The experts identified in Task 1 verified the experimental procedure, corrosion rate characterization methodology and results. Corrosion and Mechanical Durability Characterization (300oC molten sulfur) The samples subjected to isothermal testing in molten sulfur were cleaned using a multi-step procedure to remove corrosion products. First, loose deposits were brushed off, and the surfaces were glass bead blasted. The samples were then immersed in an inhibited sulfuric acid pickling solution in an ultrasonic bath, followed by ultrasonic cleaning in alcohol and acetone, and drying. After drying, the post-exposure weights of the specimens were recorded. An effective cleaning process should remove only corrosion products without stripping base metal. To quantify any cleaning-induced metal loss, replicate unexposed control specimens were subjected to the same cleaning procedure. The weights of the control specimens before and after cleaning were compared, and this correction factor was applied to adjust corrosion mass-loss values for the exposed specimens. The applicability of weight-loss measurements to quantify corrosion rate depends on how effectively corrosion products are removed. To verify the efficacy of the cleaning Page 26 of 87 DE-EE0009329 Element 16 Technologies, Inc. process, corrosion buildup on flat-welded coupons was analyzed by scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS). Figure 1 shows elemental analysis at three stages: before exposure, after corrosion testing, and post-cleaning. Across all materials, corrosion product buildup after exposure significantly increased the apparent sulfur signal and suppressed peaks from underlying elements such as iron. Post-cleaning EDS confirmed that bead blasting and chemical cleaning removed the majority of corrosion products.
